extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations (PR managers, communicators, and organizational leaders)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and evaluating public relations programs using a systems-theory perspective: monitoring environmental change, defining publics and system boundaries, choosing reactive vs proactive approaches, and using feedback/cybernetic control for organizational adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracking trends and issues / early-warning radar
rubrics_metrics.description: Be systematic in the tracking and management of issues so management can anticipate trends and issues likely to affect the organization and its publics rather than waiting to react defensively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an early-warning 'radar' to anticipate fast-moving changes (starship Enterprise metaphor). If PR does not do systematic issue-tracking, someone else in the organization will; it is a prerequisite for organizational survival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the organization–publics system appropriately per situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Publics are abstractions defined by the public relations manager; different publics (and therefore different system boundaries) must be defined for each situation or problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose publics based on the program goal (e.g., recruiting high-GPA students vs raising money for a digital media center). Interest and involvement, not only geography, can define the system components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment and adaptation to environmental change
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations must respond to change pressures by adjusting goals, structures, or processes; public relations is charged with keeping organizational relationships in tune with environmental inputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adaptation can mean redirecting mission (March of Dimes example) or changing governance/operations (American Red Cross reforms). Unmanaged responses lead to disorder (entropy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open versus closed systems (extent of interchange with environment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify systems by amount and quality of interchange with their environments: closed systems have impermeable boundaries and fail to adapt; open systems exchange inputs/outputs and are more likely to survive and grow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how permeable the organization's boundaries are to matter, energy, and information; open systems are 'especially adroit' at responding to change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reactive versus proactive public relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reactive programs employ relatively closed-systems approaches—activate only when disturbed; proactive programs use early-warning monitoring to gather information, make adjustments, and generate outputs to prevent problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactive example: California Pistachio Commission asking for inspections and lowering allowable mold levels. Reactive example: routine news releases and defensive tactics (cuttlefish/inclination to 'squirt ink').

rubrics_metrics.name: Functionary versus functional role of public relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Functionary PR attempts to preserve/promote a favorable image by supplying information to the environment only; functional PR supplies feedback to the organization, participates in decision-making/advisory roles, and seeks mutual change in organization and environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A functionary is concerned mainly with how things are said and not with what is said; functional PR is involved in shaping organizational responses and strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of conflict or competition with the external environment
rubrics_metrics.description: One determinant of how much resource an organization devotes to environmental monitoring is the degree of conflict or competition with external actors, often related to involvement with and dependence on government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher conflict/competition suggests greater need for monitoring and adaptive PR strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of dependence on internal support and unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Another determinant for monitoring/resource allocation is how dependent the organization is on internal support and cohesion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations requiring high internal unity should invest more in internal communication and environmental scanning to preserve support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived rationalization of internal operations and external environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the degree to which internal operations and the external environment are believed to be rationalized (predictable and subject to planned influence); this affects the resources devoted to monitoring and the type of adaptive strategies used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the environment/operations are seen as predictable, planned influence approaches may suffice; if not, more flexible probing is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size, structure, heterogeneity, and centralization of the organization
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization's size, structural complexity, membership heterogeneity, diversity of goals, and centralization of authority influence monitoring effort and adaptability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger, heterogeneous, decentralized organizations may need different PR structures/processes for scanning and response than small centralized ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the cybernetic control loop (goals, outputs, feedback, comparison, correction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply a cybernetic model: establish goals in a control center; produce outputs related to goals; collect feedback on effects; compare new state with goal state; determine and implement corrective outputs as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buckley's five-element model guides PR planning and continuous self-regulation; analogous to autopilot and thermostat examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify and respond appropriately to feedback (negative vs positive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feedback can be negative (error message prompting reduction/counteraction of deviation to maintain stability) or positive (amplifying deviation to promote growth/morphogenesis); PR must choose responses aligned with desired outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative feedback maintains steady state; positive feedback fosters learning and structural change. Use the type of feedback to decide whether to 'cut back' or 'increase/maintain.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Homeostasis versus morphogenesis (maintain goal states or change structure/process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize when the objective is to maintain dynamic goal states (homeostasis) versus when to pursue purposive structural and procedural change (morphogenesis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural/process changes (morphogenesis) may be necessary even when goal states remain constant; choose adaptive strategies based on feedback and environmental pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select the appropriate system level (subsystem versus suprasystem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the level of analysis appropriate to the concern: the organization and its publics may be a subsystem of a larger suprasystem, and the system boundary should reflect the problem context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: local Red Cross chapter as a local system, national Red Cross as component of national/international charity system; analysis level affects strategy and stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active environmental scanning and probing (anticipation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sophisticated/open systems actively monitor and sometimes probe their environments to detect and predict changing conditions and to initiate corrective actions before problems escalate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare to smart buildings and Wind Surf example: anticipate changes and act proactively rather than waiting for inputs to penetrate a closed boundary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indiscriminate, routine outputs as default responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not default to an output stream of news releases, email blasts, and blog postings applied indiscriminately from situation to situation; such routine defensive tactics indicate closed-systems thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor communications to the threat and context; avoid the 'tell our story' reflex without considering what the actual threat is and what type of organization change may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance internal and external outputs based on goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether PR outputs should be directed internally to change or maintain organizational goal states or externally to change/maintain environmental conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The output focus (internal vs external) depends on which option more effectively helps the system maintain or achieve its goals in the context of environmental change pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use preemptive stakeholder engagement and collaborative responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Design preemptive responses and stakeholder partnerships to address emerging public concerns and influence industry practices before crises occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Whole Foods partnering with Global Animal Partnership to create color-coded labeling, and corporate education/adoption programs that address social concerns proactively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and strategic foresight in adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Timely, strategic adjustments (buying cleaner coal early, installing scrubbers) can lock in advantages and reduce long-term costs; delayed action can be far more expensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate PR strategies for their timing and long-term orientation; proactive investments can yield cost and reputational benefits compared to reactive, delayed responses.
